study.title: 1 Chronicles 29 David, the voluntary offering, and the transition to Solomon
study.overview: The chapter closes David's reign with a focus on three movements: generous preparation for the house of God, the spontaneous response of the people, and the orderly passage of the government to Solomon. The text shows David not as one centered on himself, but as a leader who recognizes that everything belongs to the Lord, that the work of the temple is of God and that the heart of the people also needs to be directed by God. At the same time, the chapter links the construction of the temple to public worship, to national unity and to the continuity of the divine promise.

outline.title: David summons offerings to the house of God
outline.explanation: David recalls that Solomon was chosen by God for a great work, and presents his own example of abundant contribution. Then Israel's leaders voluntarily offer large amounts and precious materials, showing a generous and united response to the temple construction.

outline.title: Prayer of praise and surrender to the Lord
outline.explanation: David blesses God publicly, exalting his sovereignty over all that exists. He acknowledges that the offerings came from the hand of God and asks that the LORD preserve the voluntary disposition of the people and give Solomon an integrityful heart to obey and build the house.

outline.title: Adoration, sacrifices and confirmation of Solomon
outline.explanation: The congregation responds with praise, prostrance and sacrifice. Then Solomon receives the royal investiture again, is recognized as king, and God magnifies him before all Israel, confirming the transition of reign with honor and prosperity.

outline.title: Final summary of David's reign and death
outline.explanation: The chapter concludes with a summary of David's reign: duration, place of government, death in good age and succession by Solomon. The text also points to the historical sources consulted and presents David as the center of the events of his time.

study.context: The chapter takes place at the close of David's reign, when the leadership of Israel meets for the preparation of the temple and for Solomon's confirmation as king. The notes highlight that the contribution of the leaders recalls the voluntary offer associated with the construction of the tabernacle, and that the chronicler presents a stylized conclusion of David's reign, similar to abstracts used for other kings. The historical focus of the chapter, therefore, is not only administrative, but also cultual: the real succession is narrated in connection with the worship and the work of the house of the LORD.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that God is the owner of all things, including the riches used in worship, and that the true offering is born from the voluntary and integrityful heart. David's prayer shows that the greatness of the kingdom belongs to the LORD, not to the human king. There is here a theology of stewardship: the people return to God what they have received from it. The spiritual dependence of the leader also appears: Solomon can only fulfill his mission if God gives him an obedient heart. The real succession, the joy of the people and the sacrifices point to an order in which politics, worship and obedience to God are linked under his sovereignty.

scholarViews.insight: The chronicler points out that the weight of the temple construction fell not only about Solomon; David and the leaders of Israel also generously contributed to the work.
The offer of the leaders was made spontaneously, and the generosity of the people is presented as a free heart response, not as imposition.
David's statement points out that the palace or house is not for man, but for the name of the Lord God, emphasizing the sacred character of the work.

questions: What does this chapter reveal about the correct way to give to God: by obligation, ostentation or voluntarily with the heart?
How does David's prayer correct our tendency to think what resources, positions and capacity belong to ourselves?
How does Solomon's leadership depend, in this text, not only on political succession, but on the action of God in his heart?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to examine the origin of all that he possesses and to practice generosity with joy, recognizing that God has already given us first. He also invites to pray for leaders and successors, asking them to have an upright heart to obey the Lord. In the life of the church, this translates into service, contributions and planning made with gratitude, without manipulation or pride, but with sincere adoration and dependence on God.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not clarify in detail the exact identity of the coins of verse 7 or the nature needs some mentioned materials; therefore, it is not appropriate to speculate beyond the text. Nor should one treat as an indisputable fact the more specific reading of the term translated by 'palace' in verse 1, as this appears only as an interpretation of a commentator. The historical references to the books mentioned at the end of the chapter are given by the text itself, but it is not possible, with the notes provided, to check beyond its composition or date.
